title: “the northern army” — who or what is it?
summary: Joel 2:20 has the Lord promise to “remove far off from you the northern army”. Joel 1:6 describes “a nation … come up upon my land”, and 2:25 names the cankerworm, caterpiller, palmerworm and locust as “my great army which I sent among you”. The verses do not say whether the northern army is the same as these.
text: KJV Joel 2:20: “I will remove far off from you the northern army”. KJV Joel 1:6: “a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number”. KJV Joel 2:25: “my great army which I sent among you”. KJV Joel 2:11: “the Lord shall utter his voice before his army”.
reasoning: The northern army is not named, and the verse that names it gives a direction, north, and a fate, driven into a barren land, with “his stink” going up. The passage also calls the locust and its kin “my great army” at 2:25 and uses “army” of the Lord’s host at 2:11. It does not say that the northern army is the locust, a human army, or the Lord’s host. Possible readings, named only as readings: the swarm of insects of chapter 1, described by direction; a human army from the north; a figure of the day of the Lord. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more. It does not examine the published entry on locust and army imagery (the entry exp-late-28-2-4), which compares Joel 2:4 and 2:25 and does not ask who the northern army is.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: I will remove far off from you the northern army

title: “the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad” — where is Sepharad?
summary: Obadiah 1:20 has “the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad” possess “the cities of the south”. The verse does not say where Sepharad is.
text: KJV Obadiah 1:20: “And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel shall possess that of the Canaanites, even unto Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad, shall possess the cities of the south.”
reasoning: The verse names two groups of exiles, the host of Israel who take the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the captivity of Jerusalem “in Sepharad”, who take the cities of the south. The verse gives a name for the place of the second group and no other detail of it: not its direction, not its distance, and not its ruler. Possible readings, named only as readings: a place named by the verse that a later reader identifies by outside sources; a place the verse’s first readers knew by that name. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the one verse quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek (the Greek of this verse prints a different name and is the subject of a separate T record), does not use outside sources, and does not claim that no other passage says more. A word search of the packaged KJV, whole word and case-sensitive, found the name only at this verse.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad

title: “until the time that she which travaileth hath brought forth” — who is she?
summary: Micah 5:3 has the Lord give them up “until the time that she which travaileth hath brought forth”, after 5:2 speaks of one who is to come forth out of Bethlehem. The verse does not say who she is or whom she brings forth.
text: KJV Micah 5:3: “Therefore will he give them up, until the time that she which travaileth hath brought forth”. KJV Micah 5:2: “out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel”. KJV Micah 4:10: “Be in pain, and labour to bring forth, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail”.
reasoning: The verse names a woman by her act, travailing and bringing forth, and ties the giving up to the time of it. The passage does not say whether she is the mother of the ruler of 5:2, whether she is the daughter of Zion who is told at 4:10 to labour like a woman in travail, or whether the travail is a figure. Possible readings, named only as readings: the mother of the one who comes forth at 5:2; Zion or the people personified; a figure of the pain of the time before the deliverance. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted.
